speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: I think they were using the words in a different meaning. I do not believe that is what the Brookings Institution meant by "productive capacity." They were talking about factory equipment and the like.

Perhaps my hon. friend would like me to read the quotation. These matters are of vital interest. It is with such material that I do my thinking and, no doubt, my hon. friend does his, so that if he will pardon me I shall read this passage. It is important to be thinking about a way of putting the people back to work, of remedying unemployment. It is an idea which is quite prevalent among thinkers to-day, that we should be able, in a country like this, either to give people all they need or to put them to work. The quotation to which I refer is from the Technical Possibilities of Increased Production, in a book entitled The Condition of Great Britain, by G. D. H. Cole; it is to be found on pages 266 and 267:
The Brookings Institution estimates. . . at height of boom, American industry was working at only about four-fifths of the actual productive capacity of available factory plant and labour, and that without any improvements in technical efficiency, most industries could then have increased their output by as much as thirty per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: They are talking about industrial plant capacity which is a different matter from national capacity for production.

The very first thing you look to when you begin to wonder about the possibility of giving the people a decent standard of living is the capacity of your clothing factories, your ability to produce coal, your lumber resources, and so on, the means whereby you provide food, clothing and shelter, amusement, training, and all the things 51952-72J
the people require. If you find you have within the country the resources, equipment, training, organization, and distributive power by means of which you can deliver to the people, as, when and where required, the goods which will give them a decent standard of living, then you know that this aspect of the problem has been solved. In other words, the problem of production need no longer trouble you. You now have the problem of distribution to deal with. And the means of distribution is money. You need then to turn to the monetary aspect of the problem, and that is our whole contention this afternoon. That is the reason for moving this motion, that the government has not availed itself of the possibilities of the country's financial resources, the means of distribution.
Let me come back to the blood illustration. If a boy weighing 130 pounds increases his weight by twenty-six pounds, then unquestionably he should have two pounds more of blood. The trouble with Canada is that we can grow an extra twenty-six pounds of productivity, but the banker decides whether we shall have the blood, the money, or not.
Oh no.

There is no getting away from that. Not only is that so, but the borrowers in the country also decide. If I am correctly informed with respect to physical anatomy, if I were to lose four pounds of blood, by haemorrhage or some other mishap, there are cells within my body whose business it would be to set to work immediately to replenish the blood supply, and those cells do not wait until somebody comes and borrows blood and undertakes to pay it back with interest. There is a mechanism within my body-

Do not forget that you
have to visit the restaurant three times a day as well.

I am glad the hon. gentleman has made that remark. I would tell him in reply that, looking at the national body, we have the power to produce shoes and clothing, coal and other necessities, the thousand and one things which we require daily. There is no question that these things are there in abundance. They are the food. Speaking metaphorically, we have the body weight; the blood we need is money. We need more money, just as the body demands more blood.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And it gets more money.

Only if people
borrow; there is no question about that. I

Use of Canada's Financial Resources
am. glad my hon. friend takes issue with me; we shall discuss the matter as we go along. Suffice it to say that when a country like Canada is growing, if it is to be healthy, strong and vigorous, there must be some sort of practical, automatic mechanism by which the money stream is increased. What would happen if a physical body grew larger without a commensurate increase in the blood supply? It would become sickly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have machinery today, and it is operating every day.
We shall look forward to what the minister has to say in that regard, because we have not yet found out what it is. All I know is what I can read in books.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You have only to read the statutes.

Read Irving Fisher's book and you will see that in the matter of money the United States is at the mercy of 14,000 banks, if I remember rightly, and a few millions of borrowers. If the borrowers borrow, then the bloodstream in the economic system is increased; if the borrowers do not borrow, then there is no blood, no money. If the banks choose to lend, there is blood; if the banks decide not to lend, then the economic system will not get any blood, any money. And to-day our banks are not lending except to the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not true either.

I am glad to hear that; we are finding out things that we should never have known unless we came to parliament. Certainly where I come from there is no sign of any lending. I know that men cannot borrow now as they used to.
Did they have crops or products of value?
Yes; 1932 was a glowing example.
At twenty cents a bushel they could not borrow money.
We have an excellent example this year.
In 1937 did they have a crop on which to borrow money?

Yes; we have a fine example of it to-day. I know the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) will be interested in this discussion. In my constituency for example, with 55,000 lambs being fed this year, what is going to happen? They

are going to be sold at a loss. Why? Because there is not sufficient consumptive power; the lambs cannot be bought at profitable prices. So it is with any number of things. Beef can be produced in my constituency; but it cannot be sold at a profit; it cannot be sold for what it costs to produce it, any more than butter or cream or cheese or dozens of other things can be sold at a profit.
Nonsense.
There is no use saying, "nonsense" to me when I come right from there.
That does not answer the question whether these people had a crop of grain on which to borrow money.

Even if they had a good crop on which they could borrow money, by the time they had paid back all the money they had borrowed, and paid it back with interest, they would have less than when they started; they would be further in debt. The actual figures in the west will prove that. I have not the time to-night, however, to go into that question. We are getting away from the subject, and though I am glad to answer any questions that are asked, there is a limit beyond which one cannot go in a single speech.
I have made three attempts to complete this illustration of blood. We simply need more money in order to service our production. Without the money we cannot service production; production diminishes; the shelves are cluttered up, and there is depression. That is the story of every depression; everyone knows that. Let me illustrate in a general way; I shall not go into details but for the present shall confine myself to generalities. Let us say that actual production is 100 and money is 60-that is, purchasing power. Then we could increase that purchasing power by 10 and that would be not inflation, but reflation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What is the difference?

The difference is this: If 100 is production and 100 is consumption, then you have equilibrium and you should be able to prevent either rising or falling prices. But the moment purchasing power falls below 100, then you fall into depression and you have deflation, with the result that people must sell at a loss. That is the story of depression. If you increased money from 60 to 70, many people would consider that inflation. As a matter of fact it is not inflation; it is merely reflation, because you have to go a great many points further before 3rou can get to the point where you can

Use of Canada's Financial Resources
equate consumption with production. Another extremely important point to consider is this- and it bears upon the question asked by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin). If potential capacity is 150 and money is 60, you can increase that 60 to 120 and the only result will be an increase in production.
The idea prevails among many people that when you increase the quantity of money you immediately increase prices. I say you increase production. Go bo a coal mining area where the mines operate only part time; you spend double the amount on coal. Enlarge the market for the coal; does it raise the price? No; you will simply increase the production of coal. The same thing would be true throughout the country, with every industry which can produce more than it is now able to produce and sell. If your potential capacity were 150 and your money at 60, you could move it up to 150 and the result would be only reflation or stimulation. You would stimulate additional production. I have not time to quote authorities, but I have plenty of eminent authorities to the effect that that would be the case. This is a feature which people overlook entirely in the application of the social credit idea. The other day one hon. member rose in his place and entertained himself freely at our expense by suggesting that we could raise the dividend from $25 to $50, to S60, to $75. If you take productive capacity or potential productive capacity at which you can give people $25 worth of goods, we all know that by increasing their purchasing power you increase the immediate productive capacity of industry; and as the resources of the country, both natural and human, are called upon and brought into activity, so will the standard of living of the people be raised, until that goal which the chart of plenty indicated is reached. That is the way it is done.
But that was a positive promise to be fulfilled within eighteen months.

Exactly, and when the promise was given many things were assumed. It was assumed that there would be a great deal more willingness to cooperate on the part of many people than proved to be the case. Now let us not get oil the present subject. We are willing to debate the Alberta question to the limit at any time the hon. member wishes, but let us deal now with the question of inflation.
The next question arises right out of what I said a minute ago; you must have new money. There is no question about that. Hon. members will be interested in this fact. It was tremendously interesting to me. Carl
Snyder, quoted by Paul H. Douglas in Controlling Depressions at page 181, found that over a period of years, say during the last forty-five or fifty years, the productive power of industrial countries has increased three per cent per annum compounded. Now, if your productive capacity is 100, your consumptive capacity 100, and the money in circulation 100, and you do not increase the amount of money but your productive capacity increases to 103, then you would begin to have a fall in prices.
I wish the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) had stayed in his place. The trouble is that some hon. members do not stop to hear a thing through. He said a few minutes ago that those kings reduced the content of the money to make a profit. The fact is that they increased the amount of money, knowing that their people had to have more money because the productive power of the country had increased, and if there was not an increase in the amount of money there would be a fall in prices, just as there was in Great Britain in the last fifty years of the nineteenth century. Prices fell because they could not get enough gold to back up their ridiculous gold standard money, established under a Dutch system introduced in the days of William III, the same system we are trying to work now. There was a fall in prices with consequent suffering, notwithstanding that the productive power of the country was increasing tremendously. The same thing is true of Canada.
I quote a passage from Irving Fisher's One Hundred Per Cent Money, published in 1935. At page 85 he says:
In fact, a fixed volume of money-if its velocity did not vary-would, as business volume increased, result in a slowly falling price level. Therefore there Bhould in my view be a currency commission-
The Minister of Finance wanted to know how we would go about it; here is a suggestion. I am not an authority in this matter; if I were placed in a position where I had to be, I would soon take steps to become one, just as he did. He gathered authorities around him to instruct him on tariffs and other matters until he became one of the greatest authorities on tariffs on the American continent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I had to know where I was going and what I was about before I started.

And we know where
we are going. This bears it out, as clear as day:
. . . there should, in my view, be a currency commission authorized to manage the currency, including the cheque book money.

A thing which no government so far has ever tried.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Surely they have; we are doing it every day.
I am glad to hear that; still I cannot help judging by what I see.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The trouble is you read the wrong books!
I come from seeing realities; I see the poor suffering in every direction, I hear cries for relief coming from the cities-
We all do.
Well, is that not evidence that things are going wrong? What more evidence do you want? What is an economic system for if not to give people plenty?
The point of my observation was that I do not think the hon. member should assume he alone is in sympathy with those who are suffering.

Mr. Speaker, I think you could go through my remarks this afternoon with a fine-toothed comb and not find a single word indicating that I claim to be the only one in sympathy with those who are suffering. The hon. member is exceedingly unjust when he imputes such a thing to me.
Looking down through the course of English history we find there has been need of new money from time to time. The whole history of English finance indicates that. The disasters which followed the battle of Waterloo were entirely owing to mismanagement of money. An hon. member-I am not going to name him because we had a sort of understanding that we would not refer to each other personally-the other night said he never knew anyone to get something for nothing. Listen to this. This is from Controlling Depressions, by Paul H. Douglas, published in 1935. Before quoting the passage I may say that I know of only one class of people in the world to-day who get something for nothing. They are indicated clearly in this passage, found at page 181:
Finally it may be asked why private interests should be allowed to obtain the wealth which comes from the creation of monetary purchasing power in the form of bank credit. As Carl Snyder has shown, production, if we take long periods of time, has increased at a rate of approximately three per cent a year compounded. Now if the private bankers only increase the quantity of credit in the same proportion they would gather to themselves a very large gain in wealth and power. This has most certainly been the case in the past.
(Mr. Blackmore.3
Note it is not the member for Lethbridge who is saying that.
The volume of bank credit which has been built up from very small beginnings is now the property of the banking fraternity. By creating credit they have acquired a title to wealth and a claim upon the national income as real as if they had themselves built gigantic factories, railroads, utility plants, etcetera. Some idea of how much these sums amount to can be gained from the fact that if we were to take a credit total of thirty-three billions as our base, an increase of three per cent in this figure to match the increase in production would mean that in the very first year the private bankers would create one billion dollars in new credit.
When you stop to think what that would mean, Mr. Speaker, it would be as though they had discovered in a gold mine or an old vault a billion dollars of money, all minted and ready for use, and they simply took that out and put it into their own vaults as new money. Then you realize how serious the situation is. The author is quite clear about it; there is no question about his meaning.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
And he is not talking
about Canada.

Very good, but the
thing does apply to Canada; it would be interesting to see how my hon. friend could prove that it does not.
They would own this and would in fact increase their wealth by that much. As the total volume of credit rose, the absolute yearly additions would of course rise also.
Where will all the money come from for the dividends? We have a hint there.
Thus, three per cent of fifty billion would amount to 1-5 billion a year. A large part of the fruits of progress, therefore, tend to be transfererd to the private bankers because their ability to create the monetary counters enables them to claim title to the goods.
Our contention is that that sort of thing should no longer exist in any civilized country. The government should be gaining all that profit, not necessarily by having a government owned bank but by the creation of the monetary counters, just as fast as the productivity of the people calls for those counters.
My time is getting short. I greatly appreciate the interest and tolerance that have been shown by my hon. friends, but before leaving the banking system there is one thing more I should like to say. Let no one imagine that I am in any way opposed to the bankers, except in so far as they have been allowed to take over the creation of the life-blood of this country, which is of the most vital concern to Canada. That power must be taken back by the state, so that the state

Use of Canada's Financial Resources
may provide the people with the money they need. To-day the banks lend money and get money out into circulation only through the men who will borrow. The mere fact that they have been transferring their deposits, from people all over the country, into government securities, is clear evidence of that. They cannot and will not trust the farmers, the manufacturers and others. They want their money where it is secure. So they create their money and lend it to the country, and fasten themselves as leeches upon the body economic of this dominion, to sap the very life-blood from the people; and we allow them to do it and apparently think it all right.
We must have a means of distributing purchasing power debt free, so that it will not depend upon the fortuitous circumstance of more or less borrowers in a given community. The present system, as it is conducted, checks production and consumption, rendering it impossible for the producers to sell their goods and therefore impossible for them to produce more, thereby lowering the standard of living in this wonderful country instead of raising it. The system creates only debt, stagnation, poverty and despair in a land of potential abundance. It is an abuse that screams to high heaven. Hon. members on the government side have talked of the need of preserving the old order, of the sacred trust and responsibility that rests upon them. I admire them for those sentiments, but let me urge upon them that they have an equally great responsibility and an equally sacred trust to bring in the new order before it forces itself upon them.
May I ask the hon. gentleman a question ?

I should like, if I may, to be allowed to finish. Later I shall be very glad to answer any question my hon. friend cares to ask, but at the moment I should prefer to finish what I have to say.
At the present time all over the Anglo-Saxon world we are industriously trying to put new wine into old bottles, and it simply will not work now any more than it would in the days of the Saviour. The result is that we are changing altogether too slowly. Roosevelt expressed a thought which I believe applies very well to our situation, in his Constitution Day speech. I hope to have time to read it before six o'clock. I have culled some quotations from that speech, which I believe apply not only to the government but to me and the other members of this parliament. This is not solely your responsibility; it is mine as well, and I know you realize that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Would my hon. friend permit me to interrupt for a moment? If he intends to conclude before six o'clock, we might have an understanding that I would ask the Speaker to call it six o'clock at the conclusion of my 'hon. friend's remarks, if he does not intend to go much beyond that.
I should like to finish before six o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is, of course, perfectly free to go on as long as he wishes.

I understand that, and I appreciate it very greatly, but I think I have burdened the house quite sufficiently for this time. Among other things President Roosevelt said:
In our generation a new idea has come to dominate thought about government-the idea that the resources of the nation can be made to produce a far higher standard of living for the masses if only government is intelligent and energetic in giving the right direction to economic life.
That idea-or more properly that ideal-is wholly justified by the facts. It cannot be thrust aside by those who want to go back to the conditions of ten years ago or even preserve the conditions of to-day. It puts all forms of government to proof. . . .
Modern history proves that reforms too long delayed or denied have jeopardized peace, undermined democracy and swept away civil and religious liberties.
May I pause here to make the observation that the mere development of strains and stresses throughout this dominion, the threats of fascism and communism, are glaring evidences that reform has been too long delayed already in this country.
Yes, time more than ever before is vital in statesmanship and in government-in all three branches of it.
We will no longer be permitted to sacrifice each generation in turn while the law catches up with life. We can no longer afford the luxury of twenty-year lags.
You will find no justification in any of the language of the constitution for delay in the reforms which the mass of the American people now demand.
Yet nearly every attempt to meet those demands for social and economic betterment has been jeopardized or actually forbidden by those who have sought to read into the constitution language which the framers refused to write into the constitution.
So, Mr. Speaker, those people who have been rejoicing over the disallowance of the Alberta acts, where Alberta has striven to solve this problem for itself, realizing that the central government has neglected its trust, must remember that the selfsame device of hiding behind the constitution has been ap-

Use oj Canada's Financial Resources
plied across the line and in other countries when they have sought to bring about reforms. I continue reading:
But tolerance and fair play would disappear here as it has in some other lands if the great mass of people were denied confidence in their justice, their security and their self respect. Desperate people in other lands surrendered their liberties when freedom came merely to mean humiliation and starvation. The crisis of 1933 should make us understand that.
I believe this government should begin to issue currency and credit in terms of public need, just as the people of this dominion were led to believe it was going to, and as it has signally failed to attempt to do. It should commence to battle the money power, just as the Prime Minister said it would. Even yet the commencement of that conflict is being delayed and delayed until to-morrow.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, although it pains me in some ways to have to do so, I find myself obliged by the position and the responsibility which I hold to move a vote of want of confidence in the government on the ground that it has failed adequately to use the resources of this country to battle poverty.

Mr. ERNEST BERTR'AND (Laurier) moved the second reading of Bill No. 26, to repeal the Companies' Creditors Arrangement Act, 1933.
He said: The purpose of this bill is to repeal the Companies' Creditors Arrangement Act which was passed in 1933. The act was passed unanimously at that time as it was felt it was needed because of the state of business in the country. I have read the debates that took place, both in the house and before the committee. The discussion in the house takes up only a page and a half of Hansard. I think everyone on both sides of the house admitted at that time that this was a most important piece of legislation. The Bankruptcy Act was passed in 1919, and section 13 could have been applied to the condition sought to be corrected by the Companies' Creditors Arrangement Act. Section 13 reads:
Where an insolvent debtor intends to make a proposal for,-
(a) a composition in satisfaction of his debts; or,
[Mr. Blaekmore.l
(b)	an extension of time for payment thereof ; or,
(c)	a scheme of arrangement of his affairs; he may, either before or after the making of a receiving order against him-
That section contained subsections which were designed to take care of all arrangements that might be made before a receiving order or an assignment had been made. The section was amended in 1923 when the words " either before or" were struck out. This amendment was made because at that time there was no superintendent of bankruptcy and it was considered too easy for anyone to be appointed a trustee. It was known that in large centres like Montreal and Toronto trustees would go around to interview a company or a man who was being sued and try to induce it or him to make an arrangement with the creditors under section 13 of the Bankruptcy Act. This condition became so bad that the act had to be amended. Later on Mr. Reilly was appointed superintendent of bankruptcy and he succeeded in clearing up the situation. A reading of the discussion that took place in 1933 when the Companies' Creditors Arrangement Act was passed will show that no mention was made of section 13 of the Bankruptcy Act.

We feel that this act should be repealed as it grants to companies a privilege not enjoyed by individuals. As I say, there was no mention in 1933 of the bankruptcy law as it stood in 1919. In my opinion, this legislation was very badly drafted. I would be bold to put forward just my own opinion, so I should like to read some other opinions I have received. The Saint John, New Brunswick, board of trade passed the following resolution on F ebruary 15, 1937:
Finally we would recommend that the Companies' Creditors Arrangement Act be repealed. It was enacted during the recent business depression largely to assist debtors during those difficult times. As the business world is once again at normal levels, we submit that there is no longer any justification for the loose provisions of this statute.
The board of trade of Montreal also passed a resolution in 1937 dealing with the same matter. It reads:

Companies' Creditors Act
This legislation was enacted at a time when the economic strain of the past several years was bearing heavily on trade and was designed to relieve the heavy expense incidental to bankruptcy.
To some extent it succeeded, but to-day there exists among creditors a manifest objection to the act.
Chief among the reasons for this opposition are absence of adequate control of debtors' affairs and the consequent use of this act in order to evade the more strict and exacting provisions of the Bankruptcy Act. In explanation it should be stated that arrangements or settlements are made at metings of creditors. No trustee or inspectors are appointed, no list of creditors is required to be- issued, no examination of debtor is required, all permitting a condition not generally conducive to the protection of the creditors' interests.
It is unfortunate that in amending the Bankruptcy Act, parliament in 1923 removed a provision for settlements and arrangements without bankruptcy which existed in section 13 of the 1919 Bankruptcy Act.
The restoration of such a provision would enable all the benefits now possible under the Companies' Creditors Arrangement Act to be included in the Bankruptcy Act with the added advantage, the importance of which cannot be too strongly emphasized, of proper control by creditors and final supervision by the superintendent.
I know that complaints against this legislation have accumulated in the office of the superintendent of bankruptcy. This is quite easy to understand. As is mentioned in the resolution of the Montreal board of trade, this law has no machinery with which to protect the creditors. According to section 17, general rules were to be passed by order in council, but to date they have not been put into effect. Section 11 defines a debtor, and I should like to read subsection 2 of that section. I believe that most of the complaints are in connection with this particular section which deals with the admission of claims. If a company is in difficulty and the creditors want to come to its aid and are willing to compromise, there is always some kind of understanding between the company and the creditors asking for that compromise. It cannot be otherwise in practice, and the main question always is, Who is the bona fide creditor and who is not? Subsection 2 of section 11 reads as follows:
Notwithstanding anything contained in subsection one the company may admit the amount of a claim for voting purposes under reserve of the right to contest liability on the claim for other purposes.
That is an open door to fraud, and it has been used in a flagrant way for fraud. It is easy to understand, when a company may admit any claim for purposes of voting, reserving its right to have the claim set aside when the time for the distribution of moneys
comes, that officials of companies which want to get rid of creditors will have no difficulty in securing a sufficient number of claims for purposes of voting.
I should like to give the house figures on the number of companies that have petitioned to come under this act. In 1935 in Montreal, according to the registrar's office, fifty-five companies made application; in 1936, fifty-two; in 1937, thirty-one; and up to the third of March, 1938, there were eight. So the figures in those years respectively were fifty-five, fifty-two, thirty-one and eight, of companies making application. This, I think proves that business is getting better, and when the board of trade of Saint John, New Brunswick, says that this law was of a temporary nature,
I think the facts prove that it is so.
Now let me give the figures of companies in Toronto making application to come under the act. In 1936 there were five companies in Toronto, as reported by Dun & Bradstreet, and fifty-two for the same year in Montreal; in 1937, five in Toronto, and thirty-one in Montreal; in 1938 up to the third of March, three in Toronto, and eight in Montreal. There were a few applications made in other cities, but very few as compared with Toronto and Montreal; and if the figures for Montreal are larger than those for Toronto, it is not that we want to boast about this large number of insolvent companies. I am quoting these figures just to show the great interest that business men have in this question.

speechtext:
The figures have been given to me by the business men of Montreal, and they show that in Winnipeg, according to Dun & Bradstreet. there were no applications in 1936, and in British Columbia for the same year, according _ to Dun & Bradstreet, there was one application. I have no figures for other cities.
I should like to quote from a memorandum prepared by the board of trade of the city of Toronto. The Toronto board of trade seems to be concerned mostly with one side of the question, that with this act on the statute book, securities could be sold in different states where they would have been barred if the trust deed or the bonds had contained a proviso that the majority of the secured creditors could force an arrangement upon the minority secured creditors. That seems to be the principal reason why these gentlemen are opposing the repeal of the act. According to their own memorandum, the act requires so much reconstruction that I think it is far better .to repeal it. As a matter of
Companies' Creditors Act

fact, Mr. Speaker, we are in this situation to-day, that we have an act which the consensus of opinion of the business men of Toronto, Montreal, Saint John and everywhere else says is having very bad results, and we have either to supplement the act by adding general rules and many other sections, or to repeal the act and insert a few sections in the bankruptcy law that will cure all the above difficulties. I just want to read a paragraph or two of the memorandum prepared by the Toronto board of trade:
As unsecured creditors often have only very small claims and are widely scattered throughout the country


That is not absolutely true, but I am reading it as it appears here:

their difficulty has been that usually this type of creditor has not had sufficient interest at stake to warrant adequate representation and close contact with the various steps taken by debtors seeking compromises or extensions under the act. The result of inadequate unsecured creditor watchfulness has been that in all too many instances unscrupulous debtors have succeeded in effecting compromises quite unfair to unsecured creditors.
This was one of the reasons given for the passing of the act, that it would not require a trustee to supervise the arrangement. Even those who were in favour of the act realized that a trustee is needed. It is exceedingly bad to give to debtor companies or debtor persons the choice of three or four different acts under which they can make compromises or come into bankruptcy, because in practice it always works out against the creditor; for the debtor chooses the act where he will meet his creditors in the easiest way. Many company debtors to-day go under the Winding-up Act, because under that act there are no such offences as there are in the bankruptcy law. I quote again from the memorandum of the Toronto board of trade:
Although section 17 of this act contemplates that general rules of procedure thereunder would be made, none have been laid down yet.
And the act has been in force since 1934.
As proceedings under this act are more expeditious than proceedings under the Bankruptcy and Winding-up acts, it has been used extensively by financially embarrassed companies and owing to the lack of general rules of procedure thereunder, it has been applied by some debtor companies in a manner which was both unfair and detrimental to creditors.
I am continually quoting those who are supposed to be against the repeal, because if I should go to the files of those who complain and who are asking for repeal, I should find many other arguments that I could present here.
In a number of cases, companies have obtained court orders under this act summoning

meetings of creditors to consider proposals for payment of liabilities in full and copies of such orders and proposals have been sent to creditors with a proxy form made out in favour of the debtor's nominee. In many cases, neither a statement of the debtor's affairs nor a list of its creditors were sent with the proposals. As it is frequently inconvenient for creditors, particularly distant creditors, to attend meetings to consider debtor's proposals, and as there is often insufficient time between the receipt of the notice and the date of the meeting to investigate a debtor's affairs, and as a creditor may lose his vote unless he acts promptly, many creditors who have but a slight knowledge of the existing condition of the debtor's affairs, have completed and returned proxies in favour of the debtor's nominee with the intention that such proxy would be voted in favour of the debtor's proposal for an extension. During the depression, many creditors were willing to consent to an extension rather than risk either a bankruptcy or being forced to accept a compromise.
Another objection to the present act is that between the date upon which the court makes an order staying proceedings against a debtor and the date of the creditors' meeting, any debtor in the manufacturing business which desires to take advantage of its creditors may cut up or convert its readily saleable raw or bulk supplies into goods in process and thereby place itself in a position where its creditors would have difficulty in realizing upon the debtor's assets if the debtor's proposal were to be refused. Creditors should be given some control over the conduct of the debtor's business during this period.
There is no control at all in the law as it is to-day.
Careful consideration of the terms of the act does not indicate any completely satisfactory means of controlling this possibility. It is felt, however, that the provisions for appointment of a trustee, as suggested in the proposed general rules, go some distance towards controlling the debtor's affairs pending consideration of the proposal by the creditors and constitute a strong moral check on undesirable conduct by the debtor.
The act does not provide for the appointment of an independent person to give all creditors or possible creditors reasonable and proper notice of the debtor's proposal and of the meeting to consider it, or for the appointment of an independent party to receive creditors' proxies and to record creditors' votes. The act does not require statements of the debtor's affairs to be verified by affidavit and filed with the court or for a summary of such statement and a list of creditors to be sent out with the original proposal or to be submitted to the meeting of creditors. A statement of affairs prepared by the debtor but unaccompanied by any declaration as to its accuracy is generally produced at the meeting of creditors but unless some licensed trustee has been consulted by the debtor, the statement submitted often fails to classify the creditors (secured, preferred and unsecured) or to disclose the true position of the debtor's affairs.
As I said a few moment ago, we are in this situation, that if we leave this act on the statute -book, the complaints and the

Companies' Creditors Act
frauds that have been going on will continue until it is amended; and if we add to the act all the provisoes and rules that are wanted by some gentlemen in the business world, it will take probably another year before the amended law can come in force and we shall have to complain again of the act as it exists to-day and as it will remain in the meantime.
I know that some representation has been made to the government in connection with the amending of the Bankruptcy Act, but I have no authority to say whether it is to be amended or not. But a few words in section 13 as it was in 1919, the words "either before or after," and two or three sections that would replace section 13, subsections 3(c) 3(d) and 3(e) as they were from 1919 to 1923 would absolutely give the same security to any company willing to compromise with its creditors without going into bankruptcy.
Big corporations do not seem to like the word "bankruptcy." They might be bankrupt; they might owe more than all the assets combined; and yet they do not want to be termed "bankrupt." In 1919 section 13, subsection 3(e) of the bankruptcy law had a proviso stating that when proceedings are taken under the immediately preceding four subsections, that is when there was no receiving order or authorized assignment, all other applicable provisions of this act would apply, but no document in such proceeding would be headed "The Bankruptcy Act," nor would the term "bankrupt" or "bankruptcy" or "assignor" or "assignment" be applied to a person who before any receiving order or authorized assignment has been made makes a proposal for composition. This amendment would have the advantage of giving the same right to an individual as it gives to a corporation to-day under this act. For these reasons I move that the law be repealed.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. H. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St. George):
subtopic: REPEAL OP CHAPTER 36 OF THE STATUTES
speechtext:
I believe that the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Bertrand) has an entire misconception of the purpose of the act which he seeks to repeal and of the valued services which that act has given to the commercial community as a whole. As a matter of fact, for two years and a half, while I held the office of Secretary of State, only one complaint ever came to that office with regard to the administration of the Companies' Creditors Arrangement Act, and that was from the province of Quebec, where it was alleged that proper notice had not been given. When I called the attention of the judge to it, the judge showed that there had been a misconception of his order; he made his order clear, and the result was that there was no dissatisfaction in that case.
This act is not a bankruptcy act. A bankruptcy act has been used, so far as I have had experience, too frequently for the perpetration of the worst kind of frauds. It has been used for the purpose of enabling a few creditors to drive a company, often a competitor, into bankruptcy, to compel the liquidation of its assets by forced sale, and to destroy altogether the goodwill of the business. Time after time it -has been used by creditors to conjure up claims for the purposes of driving their rivals into bankruptcy without any hope of redemption.

subtopic: REPEAL OP CHAPTER 36 OF THE STATUTES
speechtext: May I ask a question?

subtopic: REPEAL OP CHAPTER 36 OF THE STATUTES
speechtext:
The hon. member can ask questions before we close the debate; he will have ample opportunity. As a matter of fact this act of which the repeal is sought, is, in simple terms, practically a reenactment of certain sections of the English Companies Act. In England, in that large business community where commercial and industrial affairs are carried on chiefly by companies, it was found necessary to insert certain clauses in the Companies Act to enable the creditors of the company to make friendly compromises with the company; and if three-quarters of the creditors of any particular class agreed, they could force a dissentient one-fourth into accepting a compromise which was approved by the court.
I have no time to-night within forty minutes to call attention to injustices I have seen perpetrated in my own experience by a minority of creditors, who, for their own personal ends, have precluded satisfactory, amicable arrangements being made between creditors and companies.
The hon. gentleman says that no rules have been formulated as provided in a certain section. The fact is that it never was intended that such rules should ibe formulated or put into force by the governor in council unless it should be found that the ordinary procedures of the court were inadequate for the purposes contemplated. In this case a thorough investigation was made of the procedure in each of the provincial courts, and we found that the proceedings for approval of a compromise, if made either by originating summons, as prevails in many of the English speaking -provinces, or by petition, or by motion, as in other provinces and especially in Quebec, would be governed by the ordinary rules of procedure prevailing in the courts; and it seemed to me better-and I still think it was far better-that in entering into provincial jurisdiction the rules of procedure which prevail in each provincial court should
Companies' Creditors Act

prevail in this case. If there is any complaint whatsoever with regard to the administration of this act in the courts, it is not because of lack of rules, because the Judicature Act prevails in the provinces except Quebec, and under it, as every lawyer here knows, the rules are ample and adequate for the purpose. In the province of Quebec, under the code of civil procedure, the rules there enacted are adequate in respect of every petition and original motion made before the court. There, if a motion is made, the parties interested may examine upon oath all parties concerned, and a judge in chambers hears all parties who wish to be heard and gives a just decision accordingly as to whether a scheme or arrangement which is come to under the act is made in good faith and is a fair arrangement for all the parties concerned.
This is not only a proceeding between the creditors as a whole and the debtor; it is a proceeding which enables any class of creditors by a majority holding three-fourths of the credits to approve a compromise as between that class of creditors and the debtor company. That is made to obviate the possibility of a small minority of any class of creditors serving their own selfish interests by holding out against a fair and equitable compromise. And that is the rule in England, as it is the rule which is prescribed by this act. In arranging for a revision of the Companies Act I would certainly have followed the English act and placed these very provisions in it. But certain lawyers of Ontario and Quebec and some others thought that it would not be possible to accomplish the end in view by drafting an act which would be within the legislative competence of the parliament of Canada.
This legislation, before its enactment, was advertised as few acts are that pass this parliament. The bill was circulated from one end of the country to the other; it was placed before commercial and financial men in every part of the dominion. The act was not drawn clumsily. I am not seeking credit for myself; but I say: Place the act before any competent lawyer or judge, and I am sure he will say that the bill was drawn with the utmost care possible in order to keep it within the legislative jurisdiction of parliament. It was based on the presumption that the rules of court which prevail with respect to procedure would be applied to every motion or petition made under the act. But in order that there might be power in the governor in council, in case it was shown that the rules in any particular court were inadequate, right was reserved to the governor in council to make rules for that purpose.
[Mr. Cahan.J
During the two and a half years which elapsed after the passing of the act before I ceased to be Secretary of State, there was no complaint from any quarter, while the mere enactment of the measure gave necessary and sufficient relief throughout the country; for when it once became known that a creditor, one out of a hundred, or two or more out of a hundred, could no longer hold out and defeat an equitable compromise in order that any creditor might obtain his own pound of flesh, or in order that he might exercise his right of dissent so as to destroy a competing company which should never be destroyed, then all creditors began to make reasonable arrangements with their debtor companies. Many were made that did not come under the act at all. Competent business men met together, and after discussion agreed to a fair compromise between the debtor company and its creditors, as they do frequently as between an individual debtor and his creditors. In so far as it made fair play necessary, it conduced to amicable and satisfactory settlements between debtor companies and their creditors.
But to return to the English act. The English have their bankruptcy law; they have their winding-up acts. There is there but one jurisdiction with respect to companies; here there are several jurisdictions, generally divided between the provincial and the dominion. And the difficulty in drafting this legislation was to draft an act which would not only apply to dominion companies but give the same relief to all provincial companies, whether organized under provincial charters or by special statutes of the provincial legislatures. And that object was attained because after a most thorough discussion, at which all parties were represented before the court, the Supreme Court of Canada on a reference held this act intra vires of the parliament of Canada. Therefore I wish to call attention to the English act and to its provisions. Section 153 of the English act provides that:
(1) Where a compromise or arrangement is proposed between a company and its creditors or any class of them, or between the company and its members or any class of them, the court may, on the application in a summary wray of the company or any creditor or member of the company, or, in the case of a company being wound up, of the liquidator, order a meeting of the creditors or class of creditors, or of the members of the company or class of members, as the case may be, to be summoned in such manner as the court directs.
There are no special rules in the English act for the summoning of the meeting; but the ordinary rules of practice under the Judicature Act apply. The same Judicature Act

Companies' Creditors Act
is in force, I think, in every province except Quebec, and those who are acquainted with the code of civil procedure in Quebec know that ample provision is there made for the summoning of all parties interested in order that they may be represented before the court which assumes jurisdiction.
Then subsection (2) of the same English act reads:
If a majority in number representing three-fourths in value of the creditors or class of creditors, or members or class of members, as the ease may be, present and voting either in person or by proxy at the meeting, agree to any compromise or arrangement, the compromise or arrangement shall, if sanctioned by the court, be binding on all the creditors or the class of creditors, or on the members or class of members, as the case may be, and also on the company or, in the case of a company in the course of being wound up, on the liquidator and contributories of the company.
That act was passed by the parliament of the United Kingdom which had jurisdiction over the incorporation of all companies, jurisdiction not only with respect to companies in financial difficulty, between creditors and the company, but in conflicts between shareholders inter se. Therefore, as this parliament has no jurisdiction in conflicts between the shareholders of a provincial company, it was provided in this statute-and the Supreme Court of Canada held it to be a competent statute-that the provision in the provincial acts relating to conflicts between classes of shareholders should be applied in the case of a provincial company. But in respect of any conflict between creditors and the debtor company, that is entirely within the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada, and the supreme court has so held.
Now that English act provides for compromises. They may be between a class of creditors and the company, or between the creditors as a whole if there are none of a particular class outstanding. It provides that the ordinary rules of procedure of the courts shall apply, and that is what we followed in this act, with a special provision that if it were found necessary to make new rules to overcome any fault or default in the proceedings, the governor in council was given the authority to make, alter, revoke or reenact such rules, or to delegate to the judges of the court in any district the right to make new rules. There is no deficiency in the act with respect to rules.
This act was not intended as a temporary one. It was deemed necessary for the amicable adjustment of all disputes arising between creditors and the debtor companies, amicable adjustments which would obviate the necessity of driving the debtor company into bankruptcy and having its assets sold in bulk, as they were being sold in bulk, for very low prices.
I wish to call attention to the fact that I have no knowledge of the memoranda from which the hon. gentleman has read. I do not know whence these memoranda were obtained, whether they were special petitions sent to the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Bertrand) or whether he obtained them from the superintendent of bankruptcy.

I thank the hon. gentleman for this information, but it does not influence my judgment that a committee of the board of trade even in my own home city have passed a resolution of that kind. I have seen so much of the ruthlessness of creditors who happened for the time being to hold the controlling vote in dealing with debtors, when better motives and more lenient measures should apply, that I am not surprised that some of these hard-hearted men are disgruntled at the prospect of this act being retained upon the statute books.
I have not had time to examine the return brought down by the Secretary of State, but, as a matter of fact, I think it shows that less than ten companies incorporated under the dominion statutes have applied for and obtained relief under the act. That number of compromises having been filed in the returns to that department does not show a large misuse of this statute with regard to dominion companies. I do not know as to the accuracy of the figures quoted by the hon. member for Laurier; I am bound to accept them although I do not know where they came from; but in a time of great financial distress such as prevailed during the last two and a half years that I had charge of the Department of the Secretary of State I was really surprised that so few cases arose.
The reason so few cases came up was that when a minority of the creditors of any class, that is, representing less than twenty-five per cent in value, found that there was a way by which they could be compelled to give to the debtor company a reasonable compromise which would enable it to pay its debts and retain its property for future industrial or
Companies' Creditors Act

commercial business, such minority readily entered into that reasonable compromise. As has been discovered in England, as indicated in the English act, where a certain proportion of all the creditors, representing at least three-quarters of the value, are willing to accept a reasonable compromise or arrangement, which is placed before a judge who after a thorough investigation approves it as being fair and equitable, then it is not unreasonable that the small dissentient minority should be compelled to come in and accept the terms that are offered to all.
I would regret very much, to see this act repealed. We had stress and strain in 1930, 1931 and 1932. The number of companies theft were ruthlessly driven into bankruptcy, without a chance of retrieving their position, was considerable. Bankruptcy frauds were prevalent, too, in those days. I have no doubt that they have been somewhat remedied by a better administration of the Bankruptcy Act; but the sole protest that came to me with respect to this act, after the bill had been distributed from the Atlantic to the Pacific, came from trustees in bankruptcy, gentlemen who had been appointed by the government as qualified trustees, who thought this act, which permitted a reasonable and amicable compromise, might take away a considerable portion of the fees they were receiving out of bankruptcies. They made their protests accordingly, some of which I have no doubt will be found in the files of the bankruptcy branch of the Department of Finance. But that has been entirely obviated. The act is being administered fairly. There may be rare cases where some judge who administers the act is not thoroughly informed as to company law, and perhaps does not fully realize the responsibilities which he assumes as the judge in charge of such an arrangement as this. It is only in such a case that a fraud could arise, because so long as you have a competent judiciary administering the act no frauds are possible under it.
I would regret the repeal of this legislation, and I would regard it as a backward proceeding at this time. Some hon. gentlemen may think the worst of the depression is over. Perhaps it is; perhaps the country is so prosperous that there will be few companies getting into financial difficulties under the present regime. But this year is not the end of all things. There may be other financial recessions or retrogressions; and if you have an act like this upon the statute books of Canada, in practically the same terms as the English act, you will find that it will afford relief to many honest debtor companies which

should be placed in a position to meet their creditors and, by amicable agreements and arrangements, arrived at in good faith, come to satisfactory terms with them. If you take that act off the statute books, you will find the same difficulties arising that arose during the recent depression, certainly during the last two or three years before this act was brought into force.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if there is one type of legislation with which I have little or no sympathy it is bankruptcy legislation, and in particular the Bankruptcy Act. As it is applied in this country that act disposes of the assets of the bankrupt at whatever price they will bring. The organization is disrupted; the good will of the company is depreciated and ultimately lost. That, I think, is a fair summary of the operation of bankruptcy legislation. When I heard the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Bertrand) suggest that certain individuals did not like bankruptcy, I wondered if there were any who did like bankruptcy proceedings, not only because bankruptcy brings about the results I have just indicated but because, in the case of an individual, for all time or in any event for a great number of years he carries the stigma of bankruptcy and there is an order following his earnings during that period.
It was for these reasons that I regarded very favourably the legislation referred to as the Companies' Creditors Arrangement Act. From what experience I have had of its operation, and from comments that have been made to me by creditors both large and small and by interested companies, I have found that it works out very fairly in its operation and that its provisions are very much appreciated.

speechtext:
The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Du-nning for committee of supply, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Blackmore.
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance): Mr. Speaker, the motion of the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) is an amendment to the motion that you leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into committee of supply. It is therefore, as the mover indicated, a vote of want of confidence.
I shall not deal with the language of the amendment, then, for the reason that while naturally it would command the support of

Use of Canada's Financial Resources
most if not all of those opposed to the government, it is really intended by the mover as a vehicle for the discussion of the financial theories advocated by the social credit group, and a discussion of the control of currency and credit in Canada generally. It is in that sense that I shall attempt to-night to discuss currency and credit in Canada. I do so with a very keen appreciation of the responsibility attaching to words uttered in relation to this subject by anyone who occupies the position of Minister of Finance, but I shall hope to avoid any mistakes or any slips by sticking as closely as I can to the text which I have set out for myself to follow.
During this session there have been frequent references to monetary reform, not only by those who profess so-called social credit principles but also by many other members. The right hon. leader of the opposition, while not very specific, stated on one occasion that we should not be incapable of making progress in monetary reform. He made general references to what had been done in Australia, New Zealand and South Africa, but he was very careful to point out that while these dominions had acted with great courage, conditions differed in different parts of the empire. He said that what was true in one dominion could not always be said to be true in another. Other hon. gentlemen have also referred to monetary policies and some have suggested various experiments in monetary reform.
First let me say that in my opinion it is unnecessary and confusing to speak about the need of enacting new laws in the field of monetary policy. Parliament has set up an institution, now controlled by the government, charged with the specific duty of regulating the volume of currency and credit in the best interests of the economic life of the nation. Those words I quote from the statute itself. That is now the function of the Bank of Canada. The bank is already in operation, and I am convinced that its directors and officers are attempting to perform their high task to the best of their ability and with a singleness of purpose that excludes all considerations except the promotion of the permanent welfare of the general mass of people in this country. Many hon. gentlemen realize what they have been doing. Some may not agree that what they have been doing is best for our country; but in order to keep the issue clear, let us agree that when hon. members advocate some experiments in monetary policy, some vague monetary reform, what they are really doing is criticizing the policy of the Bank of Canada. Of
course that is the right of any hon. member, but we will avoid confusion if we define the issue clearly.
I propose, therefore, to say something about the policy which the Bank of Canada has been following as shown, not by confidential information available to me in my official capacity, but by the bank's published statements. To make clearer the results already accomplished, I shall find it necessary to review briefly the Canadian monetary policy during the whole depression. Before doing so, however, it might be well to define our terms and to refer briefly to the methods by which the Bank of Canada can perform its primary purpose of controlling the volume of currency and credit in use.
By the term "currency" most of us refer to money in its narrower sense, that is to say, our bronze, nickel and silver coins, and our paper money. Our metallic coins are merely the small change of ordinary business transactions, the hand to hand money convenient for the purpose of making change. The volume of these coins in circulation is practically self-regulating. We issue them from the mint through the Bank of Canada in accordance with the public demand. If business activity and particularly retail trade are expanding, if prices are rising, the public will require more of them and the Bank of Canada will receive requests from the chartered banks to ship more five or ten cent pieces to the maritimes, more fifty cent pieces or more silver dollars to British Columbia, and so on. If we shipped more than the needs of business demanded, they would merely pile up on the bankers' shelves and become redundant. They constitute no real problem of monetary policy.
Paper money in Canada now consists of two types: first, chartered bank notes and, second, Bank of Canada notes. Chartered bank notes are subject to rigid limitation under the existing law as to maximum issue. That maximum will decrease year by year until 1945 when the banks will have the right to issue only up to twenty-five per cent of the amount of their paid-up capital. Bank of Canada notes may be issued by the bank subject only to the limitation that the bank must keep a reserve of at least twenty-five per cent in gold against its total note and deposit liabilities. The small denominations of Bank of Canada notes, chiefly the ones, twos and fives, constitute the large change of hand to hand circulation. In addition, Bank of Canada notes have another important function. Being legal tender they may constitue legal reserves for the chartered banks. In other words, our chartered banks

Use of Canada's Financial Resources
keep Bank of Canada notes as well as deposits in or balances with the Bank of Canada as the cash reserves which they are required to maintain against their demand liabilities, comprising both notes and deposits within Canada.
I shall not introduce the qualifications I would be required to introduce if I were dealing with the regulation of currency and credit under gold standard conditions. Contrary to what I sometimes read in newspaper editorials, we are not on the gold standard and are not subject to its deflationary or other controlling influences. We have long since cut adrift from gold. For better or for worse, for the time being at least, we are on a managed paper standard, just as is the United Kingdom. It is true that the Bank of Canada is required to keep a minimum gold reserve of twenty-five per cent of its combined note and deposit liabilities, but the value of our currency is determined not by gold but by the principles which govern managed paper standards and which may be summarized as demand and supply. So much for currency.
Now let us turn to the regulation of credit. What do we mean by " credit '' in this limited sense? For our present purpose "credit" means circulating credit or bank deposits. As everyone knows, the story of the last century or more, particularly in the Anglo-Saxon countries, is a story of the gradual rise of bank deposits to perform the monetary work of the business world. As a circulating medium bank deposits have been found to be infinitely more convenient than currency, and to-day in Canada, in the United States and in the United Kingdom, they are the vehicle by which ninety or ninety-five per cent of business transactions are effected. As they are in quantity the most important by far of all our circulating media, and moreover, since they are subject to wide swings of expansion and contraction, it is the control of their volume to which we mainly refer when we speak of the central bank's function of controlling the volume of currency and credit in use.
I come now, Mr. Speaker, to the methods by which the central bank exercises this power of regulation and control. These methods will warrant careful study by all hon. members, but here I can do little more than refer to them.
Briefly stated, the Bank of Canada exercises its control over the chartered banks by operating on the cash resei /es of the banking system, either by conducting so-called open market operations or by altering its rediscount rate, or by both. Our chartered banks, like all commercial banks, are accustomed to keep

a certain proportion of cash as reserves against their note and deposit liabilities. In practice they have found it necessary to keep this cash reserve in order to be able to meet the demands for cash that may be made upon them at any time by their note holders or by their depositors. In Canada the cash reserves of our chartered banks consist of notes of the Bank of Canada and deposits by the chartered banks with the Bank of Canada. Speaking of the banks as a whole, the proportion or .percentage of cash which the banks keep is in practice about ten per cent, and by law it must be at least five per cent. The Bank of Canada can expand or contract these collective chartered bank reserves at will, always providing that it can buy and sell securities or other suitable assets when it wants to. It is the buying and selling of securities for this purpose by the Bank of Canada that are commonly known as open market operations.
Suppose, for example, that the Bank of Canada buys ten million dollars' worth of securities. Then, no matter from whom it buys those securities, the reserves of the chartered banks as a whole will rise by the amount of ten million dollars. If it buys from other banks, their accounts at the central bank will be credited, and those accounts are part of the chartered banks' cash reserves. If it buys from an individual, then that individual pays the money into his account with his bank, and when that bank presents the cheque to the central bank to be paid by it, then that chartered bank's reserves at the central bank are raised by the same amount. Obviously, if each chartered bank has some percentage of cash reserves which it thinks it is necessary to maintain, the banks which eventually are credited with the additional cash and which thus find their cash reserve percentage increased, will wish to reduce it again. Otherwise they are losing the opportunity of increasing their earnings. Consequently such banks will take steps to increase their own assets and deposit liabilities by amounts sufficient to reduce their cash reserve percentages to near the customary level again.
As we have seen, the Canadian chartered banks as a group think it expedient to maintain an average reserve of ten per cent, and consequently if, as a result of the purchase of ten million dollars' worth of securities by the central bank, the reserve of the chartered banks has been increased by ten million dollars, the chartered banks will seek to expand their assets and deposits by approximately one hundred million dollars. Thus it is that security purchases by the Bank of Canada tend

Use oj Canada's Financial Resources
to expand bank deposits in the country by approximately ten times the amount of the transactions.
You may ask just how the chartered banks will expand their assets and deposits as a result of open market operations by the Bank of Canada. If the chartered banks can find good borrowers they will tend to increase their ordinary commercial loans, and by so doing increase their deposit liabilities by a similar amount. Otherwise they may buy investment securities which will usually earn them a considerably lower rate, or they may expand partly in one way and partly in the other. Either move will increase the aggregate of deposits of the banking system as a whole.
It is of interest to note that the chartered banks will all expand more or less in proportion to their relative size. Otherwise some will lose cash reserves to others and will find their individual cash reserve percentages dropping too low.
I have referred to the effect of the Bank of Canada purchasing securities. Precisely the opposite effect will ensue if the central bank sells securities. There will be a corresponding fall in the cash reserves of the chartered banks, a reduction of the average cash reserve of the banks as a group, and a consequent necessity for collective contraction of deposits on the part of the banking system.
The second well known mechanism by which the central bank exercises control is the deliberate raising or lowering of its rediscount rate. High rates, of course, tend to contract business enterprise, and low rates tend towards expansion.

The control exercised by this method is indirect rather than direct, and it may not be very effective unless there is a well developed money market sensitive to changes in discount rates. These are the major weapons which the central bank may use in carrying out its primary function of controlling the volume of credit and currency in use in the country.
In order to obtain a proper perspective from which to consider how far the bank has carried out its duties, let us glance back over the course of monetary policy during the depression. It will only be necessary to call attention to a few salient points1. We recall too keenly the vicious spiral of deflation which pursued its devastating course from the end 51952-73
of 1929 until the beginning of 1933. On December 31, 1929, Canadian deposits of the chartered banks totalled 82,270,000,000. This volume of deposits was based on a cash base of about $228,000,000, which had been expanded rapidly as a result of advances made under the old Finance Act. These advances had increased to $81,700,000 on December 31, 1929. By October 31, 1932, the cash in Canada had been reduced to $183,000,000, of which only $27,500,000 was based on Finance Act advances, and Canadian deposits had shrunk to $1,960,000,000. This represented a contraction of over fourteen per cent in circulating credit.
I shall not take time to debate the difficult theoretical problem as to whether this credit contraction was the cause or the result of the liquidation of business and the fall in prices. I shall merely state what I believe to be the prevailing view among competent economists, that while in the early stages of the depression the contraction of credit was probably largely the reflection of the decline in business and prices caused by fundamental jconomic maladjustments, yet after a time the monetary and credit factor became definitely an important cause.
From early in 1931 to the United States banking crisis in March, 1933, credit liquidation was certainly a factor operating with cumulative force to aggravate the decline in business and prices. Here was a time when, if ever, the use of monetary policy was justified as a weapon against the ravages of deflation. In my opinion, an opinion held at that time as well as now, conditions in this country were such as to warrant prompt and courageous experiments of the type which my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) apparently has now in mind. However, no action was taken until about the close of this deflationary period, in November, 1932-

the tardiness of and perhaps also the lack of vigour in his measures. I realize, of course, that the machinery which was available to his hand was inadequate and cumbersome, and that any bold and aggressive measures would have been bound to meet the strongest possible resistance from the orthodox financial world.
The expansion of bank cash, which began in November, 1932, was soon followed by a cessation of the declining trend in Canadian deposits; and when, following an amendment to the Dominion Notes Act of June, 1934, a further substantial expansion of bank cash occurred, Canadian deposits began a rapid rise which has continued until the present time. In March, 1935, the Bank of Canada commenced to operate as a central bank and assumed responsibility for the regulation of the cash reserves of the chartered banks and consequently of the volume of credit in circulation. Recognizing that the regulation of the country's credit and currency was so vital a sovereign function that it could not be left in the control of a private institution, this government in 1936 amended the Bank of Canada Act to give the dominion government effective control over the bank by majority ownership of the capital stock and majority control of the board of directors.
